snapshot.title: Cognitive Reappraisal and Acceptance
snapshot.design: Within-person sad films with randomized reappraisal/acceptance instruction order; two-minute films and two-minute recovery.
snapshot.population: Eligible lab completers: 77 first-year US students; 65 community adults. Physiology film/recovery n=55/42 and 51/48 respectively.
snapshot.accessDepth: Selected published full Methods, outcome Results and Discussion; author-hosted PDF. Inspected primary record: https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5c2cdcb88f51304e8d797515/t/5c6dae31a4222f35736fcb1d/1550691890403/reappraisal%2Bacceptance.pdf
snapshot.summary: During films, reappraisal reduced sadness and increased positive affect more than acceptance; acceptance was rated less difficult. Sample 1 negative-emotion composite and recovery self-report comparisons were nonsignificant. Acceptance showed less SCL dampening during Sample 1 films; its recovery comparison did not reach significance (p=.06), and no statistically significant SCL difference was detected in Sample 2. Perceived difficulty is not objective cognitive load; physiology and reported emotion differ. Acute comparisons do not establish longer-term clinical benefit or social transfer.
snapshot.sampleSizeNote: Eligible lab completers: 77 first-year US students; 65 community adults. Physiology film/recovery n=55/42 and 51/48 respectively.

snapshot.title: Measuring actual learning versus feeling of learning
snapshot.design: Individually randomized crossover across two consecutive classes; active problem solving versus passive lecture, matched content and handouts. End-of-class feeling survey followed by 12-item multiple-choice test.
snapshot.population: 149 participating/completing students across two Harvard introductory physics courses; 8 of 157 opted out or did not complete.
snapshot.accessDepth: Selected full-text methods/results, Tables 1–3 and relevant discussion in institutional-hosted primary article; supplementary file not read. Inspected copy: https://www.williams.edu/teaching-center/files/2023/09/Deslauriers-et-al.-2019.pdf
snapshot.summary: Active instruction produced higher immediate physics test scores but lower perceived learning than passive instruction. No delayed retention or transfer was measured. A feeling of learning can diverge from measured performance without being universally misleading.
snapshot.sampleSizeNote: 149 participating/completing students; 8 of 157 opted out or did not complete.
